pos: n. (the cover of a house; in Israel a flat and usable surface; rendering Hebrew gag, Greek stege)
etymology: From the Saxon hrof, a roof or top. The biblical roof is not the pitched roof of northern Europe but the flat gag of a near-eastern house — a working floor reached by an outside stair, where flax was dried, guests were lodged, and men walked in the evening.
biblical_def: The roof of a biblical house is a room in the open air, and the law required it to be safe: “When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence” (Deuteronomy 22:8). That is a remarkable statute. God legislates a parapet, and makes a builder answerable for a stranger's fall — the sixth commandment reaching into carpentry, and negligence counted as bloodguilt. The roof is also where Rahab hid the spies, having “brought them up to the roof of the house, and hid them with the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof” (Joshua 2:6) — a harlot's workaday roof becomes the shelter of Israel's scouts and her own house the one spared. The Gospels twice make the roof the place of faith. Friends who could not reach Christ “uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay” (Mark 2:4) — the Lord saw their faith in the damage they were willing to do. And a Roman officer refuses the honour of a visit: “Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof: but speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed” (Matthew 8:8). Christ marvelled, and said he had not found so great faith in Israel.
webster_summary: The flat, usable cover of a house. The law requires a parapet and counts a fall as bloodguilt; Rahab hides the spies on hers; a paralytic is let down through one; a centurion says he is unworthy that Christ come under his.
webster_full: ROOF, n. [Sax. hrof.] The cover or upper part of a house or other building, consisting of rafters covered with boards, shingles or tiles.
2. A vault; an arch; or the interior of a vault; as the roof of heaven.
3. The palate, or upper part of the mouth; as the roof of the mouth.
4. ROOF, v.t. To cover with a roof.
5. To inclose in a house; to shelter.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 22:8 is filed away as quaint ancient building code, when it is the sixth commandment applied to construction — a standing testimony that negligence which endangers a neighbour is a moral matter.
corruption_paragraphs: The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel are not binding on the church in their form, and no Christian is required to build a parapet in a climate where nobody walks on a roof. But the moral law they express does not expire, and Deuteronomy 22:8 states it as plainly as any verse in Scripture: a man who builds where others will walk is answerable for what happens to them. God calls the consequence blood upon thine house, which is the language of the sixth commandment, and he attaches it not to malice but to an omission — a railing that was not built. A conscience formed by this verse will treat safety, maintenance, and honest workmanship as obedience rather than as liability management.

The principle to recover is the roof in Mark 2. Four men carried a friend, found the house impassable, climbed the outside stair, and dug through another man's roof to reach Christ — and the text says that Jesus, seeing their faith, spoke to the paralytic. Faith is credited to the ones who did the digging. Set beside the centurion, who would not have the Lord cross his threshold at all, the two roofs frame the whole range of faith: one tears a house open to get to him, the other will not presume on him for a moment, and he commends both.
roots_summary: Hebrew gag is the flat roof of a house, a usable space. Greek stege is a roof or covering; doma is the housetop from which the gospel is to be proclaimed.
roots_lines: Hebrew gag (H1406) — the flat roof of a house or of the altar; a place of work, sleep, and prayer.
Hebrew maaqeh (H4624) — a parapet or battlement; the railing commanded in Deuteronomy 22:8.
Hebrew aliyyah (H5944) — an upper chamber, often built upon the roof; the prophet's lodging.
Greek stege (G4721) — a roof; the centurion's word in Matthew 8:8.
Greek doma (G1430) — a housetop; preach ye upon the housetops, Matthew 10:27.
usage: Of the law of the parapet: thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof (Deuteronomy 22:8).
Of faith that broke through: they uncovered the roof where he was (Mark 2:4).
Of faith that would not presume: I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof (Matthew 8:8).

pos: n. (a covered entrance or colonnade before a building; rendering Hebrew ulam, Greek stoa and proaulion)
etymology: From the Latin porticus, a colonnade, from porta, a gate. Hebrew ulam is the vestibule standing before the temple proper — the threshold space a worshipper crossed before he was inside.
biblical_def: A porch is the space before the door, and Scripture gives it more weight than an entryway usually gets. Solomon's temple had one built to scale: “the porch before the temple of the house, twenty cubits was the length thereof, according to the breadth of the house” (1 Kings 6:3). The house of God did not open directly onto the street; there was a place to arrive before there was a place to enter, and the architecture taught approach. By the New Testament the temple's eastern colonnade was called Solomon's porch, and it became the ordinary place of public teaching and controversy: “Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch” (John 10:23) — and within a few verses the Jews take up stones. After Pentecost the same colonnade is where the healed lame man held Peter and John and “all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon's, greatly wondering” (Acts 3:11). The apostolic preaching happened in the same portico where Christ had been threatened. Its most poignant appearance is Peter's: “when he was gone out into the porch, another maid saw him” (Matthew 26:71). He had drawn back from the fire toward the exit, and the second denial met him there. A porch is a place of not-quite-in and not-quite-out, and the Gospel records what it costs to linger in one.
webster_summary: The covered space before a door. The temple's porch taught approach, Solomon's colonnade held both Christ's teaching and the apostles' preaching — and Peter's second denial met him as he edged toward the exit.
webster_full: PORCH, n. [L. porticus, from porta, a gate, passage or entrance.] In architecture, a kind of vestibule supported by columns at the entrance of temples, halls, churches or other buildings.
2. A portico; a covered walk.
3. By way of distinction, the Porch, a public portico in Athens, where Zeno taught his philosophy; whence his followers were called Stoics.
4. In Scripture, the vestibule before the temple; the porch of the house, 1 Kings 6.
5. Solomon's porch, a colonnade on the east of the temple, John 10.
corruption_summary: The porch becomes a settled address rather than a threshold — a place to be associated with Christ without entering — which is the position Peter occupied on the night he denied his Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew's account traces a drift with painful care. Peter follows afar off, sits with the servants to see the end, denies once by the fire, and then goes out into the porch, where the second denial finds him. Each step is a small withdrawal, and none of them is the decisive act; the decisive act is made possible by them. The porch is where a man is close enough to be recognised and far enough to deny, and it is a real spiritual location. Congregations are full of people standing in it — attached, familiar, unwilling to be identified. The remedy is not more atmosphere in the porch but a door, and Christ says plainly that whosoever shall confess him before men, him will he confess before his Father (Matthew 10:32).

The principle to recover is that God built the porch and meant it to be crossed. The temple vestibule was a place of preparation, not of residence, and the whole design moved inward — porch, holy place, holy of holies — toward a presence that could not be approached carelessly. That approach is now opened by a better way: the veil is rent, and believers have boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19-20). It would be a strange thing to be given an opened holy of holies and to settle in the portico.
roots_summary: Hebrew ulam is the vestibule or porch before the temple. Greek stoa is a colonnade — the root of Stoic, from Zeno's teaching porch; proaulion is the forecourt of a house.
roots_lines: Hebrew ulam (H197) — a porch or vestibule; the space before the temple proper.
Hebrew misderon (H4528) — a colonnade or porch; the porch of Eglon's summer parlour.
Greek stoa (G4745) — a portico or colonnade; Solomon's porch in John 10 and Acts 3.
Greek proaulion (G4259) — a forecourt or porch; where Peter denied his Lord the second time.
Greek pulon (G4440) — a gateway or porch; the entry of a house or city.

Of the colonnade where Christ taught: Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch (John 10:23).

pos: n. pl. (rods used to fasten a gate or bind a frame; figuratively, fixed limits; rendering Hebrew beriach)
etymology: From Old French barre, of uncertain origin. Hebrew beriach is from barach, to flee or pass through — a bar is what stops the passing through, whether shot across a gate or run through the rings of a frame.
biblical_def: Bars in Scripture hold things together and hold things out. In the tabernacle they are structural: “thou shalt make bars of shittim wood; five for the boards of the one side of the tabernacle” (Exodus 26:26) — the boards stood upright and the bars ran through their rings, so that a tent of separate planks became one house. God's dwelling was engineered for unity, and the parts were held by what passed through them all. In a city, bars are security, and their strengthening is a blessing: “For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee” (Psalm 147:13). The two clauses belong together — safe gates and blessed children, defence and family in one breath. Nehemiah's rebuilders set them in place gate by gate: they “laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Nehemiah 3:3), a verse repeated like a refrain through that chapter as ordinary men finished ordinary sections. And Jonah, from the fish's belly, uses the word for the shut world of the dead: “the earth with her bars was about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O LORD my God” (Jonah 2:6). The bars were for ever, and were opened; the type our Lord applied to himself.
webster_summary: Rods that fasten or bind. In the tabernacle they make many boards one house; in a city they are a blessing set beside blessed children; in Jonah they are the everlasting bars of the grave, and they opened.
webster_full: BAR, n. [Fr. barre.] A piece of wood, iron or other solid matter, long in proportion to its diameter, used for various purposes, but especially for a hindrance or obstruction.
2. Any obstacle which obstructs, hinders or defends; an obstruction; a fortification.
3. The bar of a court; the place where prisoners are stationed.
4. A bank of sand, gravel or earth, forming a shoal at the mouth of a river or harbor.
5. In Scripture, bars of iron and brass, the fastenings of gates; I will break in pieces the gates of brass, Is. 45.
corruption_summary: Limits are treated as an insult to the self, so that every bar is read as a restriction to be broken — while Scripture makes bars a blessing, a structure, and the mark of a world God has bounded.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct that all boundaries are oppressive would have to call Psalm 147:13 a curse. There the strengthened bars of the gates and the blessed children within are one thought: without the bars the children are not safe, and a city with nothing shut is not free but exposed. Scripture is unembarrassed about limits because it holds that God set them — to the sea he said hitherto shalt thou come, but no further, and the same speech that bounds the ocean bounds a man's days and a nation's borders. Bars in the tabernacle make the same point constructively: the boards did not lose anything by being bound; they became a dwelling place for God, which no single plank could be.

The principle to recover is Jonah's. He describes bars that were for ever — the settled, unbreakable enclosure of death — and in the same sentence says God brought up his life from corruption. Our Lord took Jonah's three days as the sign of his own burial, and the New Testament announces that he has the keys of hell and of death (Revelation 1:18). The one bar that could not be broken from inside was broken from outside, which is why the church has never been able to treat the grave as final and has always buried its dead in hope.
roots_summary: Hebrew beriach is a bar or bolt, from barach, to pass through — both the bar run through rings and the bolt shot across a gate.
roots_lines: Hebrew beriach (H1280) — a bar, a bolt; the tabernacle bars and the bars of a city gate.
Hebrew barach (H1272) — to flee, to pass through; the root, from the bar that runs through the boards.
Hebrew manul (H4514) — a lock or bolt; the locks set with the bars in Nehemiah 3:3.
Hebrew metil (H4300) — a bar or rod of metal; the bars of iron and brass.

Of bars as a blessing on a city: he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates (Psalm 147:13).

pos: n. (a circle of metal; a signet worn as a token of authority; rendering Hebrew tabbaath, Greek daktulios)
etymology: From the Saxon hring, a circle. Hebrew tabbaath is from taba, to sink or impress — the ring is named for what it does, sinking a seal into wax or clay, so that its meaning is authority before it is ornament.
biblical_def: A ring in Scripture is either a fitting or a seal. In the tabernacle it is a fitting, and its purpose is portability: “thou shalt cast four rings of gold for it, and put them in the four corners thereof” (Exodus 25:12), with the standing order that “The staves shall be in the rings of the ark: they shall not be taken from it” (Exodus 25:15). The ark of the covenant was permanently ready to move. God's dwelling among a pilgrim people was never furniture. As a seal, the ring is delegated authority in metal, and Scripture uses it at the two poles of human dealing. Ahasuerus “took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews' enemy” (Esther 3:10) — a king hands over the power to seal an irrevocable decree, and a genocide is authorised by a man who never read the paperwork. And the father of the prodigal, before a word of restitution has been proposed, tells the servants: “Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (Luke 15:22). The robe covers, the shoes mark a son rather than a servant, and the ring restores authority to a man who had squandered everything.
webster_summary: A circle of metal — a fitting or a seal. The ark's rings keep it ever ready to move; a king's signet authorises a genocide; a father puts one on a returning son's hand before restitution is even discussed.
webster_full: RING, n. [Sax. hring.] A circle, or a circular line, or any thing in the form of a circular line or hoop.
2. An ornament worn on the finger; as a wedding ring; a signet ring.
3. A circle of gold or other metal used to fasten or to bear something; as the rings of the ark.
4. A circular area in which races are run or feats performed.
5. In Scripture, the king's ring, the signet by which decrees were sealed, Esth. 3.
corruption_summary: The father's ring in Luke 15 is softened into mere sentiment, when it is the restoration of authority to a son — and the same parable is used to teach a welcome that never required a return.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 15 is frequently preached as an assurance that God receives everyone as they are, which drops the hinge of the story. The son came to himself, rose, went to his father, and had a confession ready before he was met: Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight. That is repentance, and the parable is unintelligible without it. What the parable does teach, gloriously, is that repentance is met before it is finished — the father saw him a great way off, ran, and fell on his neck while the speech was still unspoken, and the ring went on a hand that had nothing to offer. Grace outruns the confession; it does not replace it.

The principle to recover is what a ring meant. It was not jewellery but a seal, the instrument by which a household's business was authorised. To put one on the prodigal's hand was to give back the standing he had cashed in — not a probationary readmission but full restoration to the family's authority. Set against Esther 3:10, where a signet is handed to an enemy of God's people and death is sealed with it, the two rings show what the same object does in different hands. And the ark's rings hold the third sense: God's house was built to travel, and the staves were never to be drawn out.
roots_summary: Hebrew tabbaath is a ring or signet, from taba, to sink or impress. Greek daktulios is a finger-ring; sphragis is the seal it makes.

pos: n. (that which is spread over a thing to hide or shelter it; rendering Hebrew mikseh and kesuth, Greek peribolaion)
etymology: From cover, through Old French covrir, from the Latin cooperio. The Hebrew family is dominated by kaphar, to cover — the same root that gives kippur, atonement. In Hebrew, to cover a thing and to atone for it are one word.
biblical_def: A covering is what is spread over, and Scripture's use of it is inseparable from atonement, because the Hebrew for covering is the Hebrew for making atonement. The tabernacle's outermost layer was deliberately plain: “thou shalt make a covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers' skins” (Exodus 26:14). Gold within, weatherproof hides without — the house of God looked like nothing from the road, which is a comment on how glory is usually packaged. When the camp moved, the holy things were covered before they were carried: “shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins, and shall spread over it a cloth wholly of blue” (Numbers 4:6). Isaiah uses the word for the futility of a self-made refuge: “the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it: and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it” (Isaiah 28:20) — a proverb about every scheme of security a man devises apart from God, which never quite reaches. And Paul gives a creational covering: “if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15). The argument of that chapter runs on headship and creation order, and the covering is a sign of a real order rather than a merely local custom.
webster_summary: That which is spread over — and in Hebrew the same root as atonement. The tabernacle's outer covering was plain hides; Isaiah makes a short covering the image of self-made security; a woman's hair is given her as a covering.
webster_full: COVERING, n. That which covers; any thing spread or laid over another, whether for security or concealment.
2. Clothing; raiment; garments; dress.
3. A cover; a lid; that which shuts in or conceals.
4. COVER, v.t. [Fr. couvrir; L. cooperio.] To overspread the surface of a thing with another substance.
5. To conceal; to hide by something overspread; also, in Scripture, to forgive; charity shall cover the multitude of sins, 1 Pet. 4.
corruption_summary: Covering is read as concealment only, so that the biblical link between covering and atonement is lost — and 1 Corinthians 11 is dismissed as a local custom with nothing to say about creation order.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis sets the pattern in one chapter. Adam and Eve sew fig leaves and hide, and their covering is concealment that fails; then God makes coats of skins and clothes them, and that covering costs a life. Every later covering in Scripture stands between those two — the self-made one that is always too narrow, and the God-given one that requires a death. This is why kaphar serves for both covering and atonement, and why the mercy seat is the covering over the ark where blood was sprinkled. To flatten the word into mere hiding is to lose the doctrine buried in the vocabulary: sin covered by God is not sin overlooked, it is sin answered for. The treatment of 1 Corinthians 11 as a purely cultural instruction fails on the apostle's own reasoning, which does not appeal to Corinthian fashion but to the order of creation — the head of the woman is the man, and the man is not of the woman but the woman of the man. Whatever the outward form in a given place, the complementarian order the sign expresses is creational and does not lapse.

The principle to recover is Isaiah's proverb, which is one of the shrewdest images in the prophets. A bed too short and a blanket too narrow describe every refuge a man builds for himself: adequate until he actually lies down in it. Judah had made a covenant with death and thought herself secure; the LORD's answer is that the arrangement will not cover her. The only covering that reaches is the one provided, and Romans states it as blessedness: blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Romans 4:7).
roots_summary: Hebrew mikseh is the tabernacle's outer covering; kesuth, a garment or covering. Behind both stands kaphar, to cover and so to atone. Greek peribolaion is something thrown around.

Hebrew kesuth (H3682) — a covering, a garment; also used of a wife as a covering of the eyes.
Hebrew kaphar (H3722) — to cover, to pacify, to make atonement; the root of kippur.
Hebrew kapporeth (H3727) — the mercy seat, the covering over the ark where blood was sprinkled.
Greek peribolaion (G4018) — something thrown around, a mantle; the covering of 1 Corinthians 11:15.

pos: n. pl. (the flanks or parts of a thing; the innermost recesses; rendering Hebrew tsad and yerekah)
etymology: From the Saxon side. The KJV's sides often renders Hebrew yerekah, which means the far parts or recesses — the hinder or innermost region — so that the sides of a ship or of the north are its depths rather than its edges.
biblical_def: Sides in the Authorized Version frequently means not edges but far recesses, and the difference matters. In the tabernacle it is plain and structural: “thou shalt put the staves into the rings by the sides of the ark, that the ark may be borne with them” (Exodus 25:14). In the household psalm it is a picture of ordered blessing: “Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table” (Psalm 128:3) — the vine trained along the inner walls, fruitfulness within the home rather than displayed outside it. In Jonah it is the hold of a ship: while the mariners cried every man to his god and threw the cargo overboard, “Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep” (Jonah 1:5). The prophet is furthest in and furthest down, asleep through a storm that his own disobedience raised, while pagans pray. And Isaiah records the most famous sides in Scripture, in the boast of the king of Babylon: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north” (Isaiah 14:13). He aims at the innermost place of the divine assembly, and the passage answers him: yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.
webster_summary: The flanks — and in the KJV often the innermost recesses. A wife fruitful by the sides of the house, Jonah asleep in the sides of the ship, and a king aiming at the sides of the north who is brought to the sides of the pit.
webster_full: SIDE, n. [Sax. side.] The broad or long surface of a body, as distinguished from the end, which is of less extent.
2. Margin; edge; verge; border; the exterior line of any thing.
3. The part between the top and bottom; the slope; declivity; as the side of a hill.
4. Party; faction; interest; as, he took our side in the dispute.
5. In Scripture, the inner or hinder parts; the sides of the north, Is. 14; the sides of the pit, Is. 14.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 14 is read as a merely political taunt, losing the pattern of prideful ascent it exposes — and Psalm 128's picture of fruitfulness centred in the home is treated as a diminishment of women.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 14:13-14 is a five-fold I will — I will ascend, I will exalt, I will sit, I will ascend above the heights, I will be like the most High — and it names the anatomy of pride wherever it appears. Whether the taunt is aimed only at a Babylonian king or reaches behind him to the fall of Lucifer, the pattern is the same and the answer is the same: the ascent ends in the sides of the pit. Reading the passage as ancient political rhetoric and nothing more removes the mirror it was meant to be. Every self-exaltation follows the same five steps and arrives at the same address. Psalm 128:3 is likewise resented, because a wife described as a fruitful vine by the sides of the house sounds to modern ears like confinement. The image is of honour, not restriction: the vine is the most valued planting a household had, trained where it would flourish, and its fruit was the family's wealth. Scripture's ordering of the home is creational, and it dignifies what it orders.

The principle to recover is Jonah in the hold. The sides of the ship are the deepest and most sheltered place aboard, and that is exactly where a fleeing prophet is found asleep while unbelieving sailors pray for their lives. Disobedience does not usually feel like a storm; it feels like sleep in a quiet place, several decks below the trouble one has caused. The shipmaster's question is the sermon — What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God — and it had to be put to the prophet by a heathen.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsad is a side or flank; yerekah is the far or innermost part — the recesses of a ship, a cave, or the north. Greek pleura is the side of the body.

pos: n. (the inner lining of a room, in the KJV panelling of wood; the Authorized Version spelling of ceiling; rendering Hebrew saphan, to panel)
etymology: From the Latin caelum or the French ciel, heaven — the inner covering of a room being its sky. The Authorized Version keeps the older spelling cieling and the verb cieled, and the Hebrew saphan means to cover or panel with boards.
biblical_def: To be cieled in the Authorized Version is to be lined with fitted wood, and it is a mark of finished, costly building. Solomon's temple is described exactly: “he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood” (1 Kings 6:15), and the Chronicler adds that “the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains” (2 Chronicles 3:5). No stone was left showing. The house of God was finished on the inside where only priests would see it, which is a lesson about work done for God in places no visitor inspects. The prophets then take the same word and turn it against luxury. Jeremiah indicts a king who builds himself a wide house “and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion” (Jeremiah 22:14) — and the charge in the surrounding verses is that he built it by unpaid labour and would not judge the cause of the poor. Haggai puts the question that gives the word its edge: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Haggai 1:4). The panelling is not the sin. The order of priorities is.
webster_summary: The inner wooden lining of a room, in the Authorized Version's spelling. Solomon panelled the temple where only priests would see; Haggai asks a people why their own houses are cieled while God's house lies waste.
webster_full: CEILING, n. [from ceil; L. caelum, heaven.] The inside lining or covering of the top of a room; the upper surface within a building.
2. CEIL, v.t. To overlay or cover the inner roof and walls of a building with boards or plaster.
3. In the KJV spelled cieling; the walls of the cieling, 1 Kings 6.
4. CIELED, pp. Lined or covered with boards; as, cieled with cedar, Jer. 22.
5. In ships, the inside planking of the hull.
corruption_summary: Haggai 1:4 is used to shame ordinary domestic comfort, or else avoided entirely — when its charge is neither asceticism nor luxury but the ordering of what gets finished first.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misreadings of Haggai are common. The first turns the verse into a rebuke of any good house, as though panelling were itself sinful and the mark of piety were a bare room. Scripture does not support it: God commanded the cedar and the gold in his own house, and the same prophet promises that the latter house's glory shall exceed the former. The second misreading buries the verse under the observation that the church is people rather than a building, which is true and is used to avoid the question. Haggai's complaint was about sequence. The returned exiles had found the resources, the craftsmen, and the time to finish their own interiors, and had concluded that the LORD's house could wait for a more convenient season. He answers by pointing at their harvests: ye have sown much, and bring in little.

The principle to recover is from Solomon's cedar. He lined the inside of the house with fitted boards and overlaid it with gold in rooms no worshipper would ever enter, because the work was for God and not for the visitors. That standard reaches into every unseen part of Christian labour — the preparation nobody audits, the accounts nobody checks, the kindness done where no one is watching. God sees the inside of the house, and the finishing of it is worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew saphan is to cover or panel with boards; saphun, cieled. The related sippun is the panelled ceiling itself, the finished inner surface of a house.

pos: n. (the meeting of two lines or walls; the extremity of a field or garment; rendering Hebrew pinnah and peah, Greek gonia)
etymology: From Old French cornere, from the Latin cornu, a horn — the projecting point of a thing. Hebrew pinnah is a corner or the chief cornerstone; peah is the edge or side, and gives the law of the corners of the field.
biblical_def: A corner in Scripture is the point where two things meet, and it carries both charity and judgment. The law of gleaning makes the corners of a field the property of the poor: “when ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest” (Leviticus 19:9). This is welfare with a plough in it — the owner leaves standing grain, and the poor come and work for it, so that provision is real and dignity is preserved. Our Lord uses the street corner to expose display: hypocrites “love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men” (Matthew 6:5), the corner being chosen because two roads see you at once. Peter's vision uses corners for the whole world's compass: a vessel “as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth” (Acts 10:11), from which he learns not to call any man common or unclean. And Zechariah makes the corner a messianic title: “Out of him came forth the corner, out of him the nail, out of him the battle bow” (Zechariah 10:4) — the corner being the stone that binds two walls into one building, which is precisely what Paul says Christ does with Jew and Gentile, being himself the chief corner stone.
webster_summary: Where two things meet. The corners of a field belong to the poor; the corners of the streets tempt to display; a sheet knit at four corners opens the gospel to the nations; and the corner is a name of Christ.
webster_full: CORNER, n. [L. cornu, a horn, a point.] The point where two converging lines meet; properly, the external point.
2. The interior point where two lines meet; an angle.
3. A secret or retired place; a private or secluded spot.
4. The end, extremity or limit; as the corners of the field, Lev. 19.
5. Corner stone, the stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone, Eph. 2.
corruption_summary: The corners of the field are cited to endorse whatever redistribution is currently proposed, dropping the law's own shape — the owner keeps his field, and the poor come and reap.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:9 is regularly enlisted on both sides of modern argument, and both readings tend to lose its form. It is not a tax, and it is not charity as we usually mean it. The field remains the owner's; what he is forbidden is to harvest it to the last stalk. The poor are not delivered a portion but come themselves and glean it, which is exactly what Ruth does in Boaz's field — she works from morning until evening, and the provision reaches her through her own labour and a landowner's obedience. Scripture's categories here are the poor and the stranger, not a class defined by grievance, and the mechanism preserves both property and dignity. Any scheme that leaves the poor idle or the owner dispossessed has departed from the model rather than applied it.

The principle to recover is Zechariah's title. Out of him came forth the corner — the cornerstone from which the walls take their line, so that everything built after it is square or crooked by reference to it. Paul says the household of God is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone, and that in him the two walls, Jew and Gentile, are fitted together and grow into an holy temple (Ephesians 2:20-21). The stone the builders rejected is the one that made the building one.
roots_summary: Hebrew pinnah is a corner or chief cornerstone; peah is an edge or side, giving the law of the field's corners. Greek gonia is an angle or corner, as in akrogoniaios, chief corner stone.

pos: a. (interior; further within; rendering Hebrew penimi, Greek eso and esoteros)
etymology: From the Saxon innera, the comparative of in. The word is always relative — an inner court presupposes an outer one — and Scripture's architecture is built in graded degrees of inwardness that teach approach to God.
biblical_def: Inner in Scripture nearly always implies a threshold crossed. Solomon's house of God was built in degrees, and at its heart: “he set the cherubims within the inner house: and they stretched forth the wings of the cherubims, so that the wing of the one touched the one wall… and their wings touched one another in the midst of the house” (1 Kings 6:27). The wings spanned the whole room, which is a way of saying that the innermost place was full. Ezekiel is carried to “the door of the inner gate that looketh toward the north; where was the seat of the image of jealousy” (Ezekiel 8:3) — and the horror of that chapter is precisely that the idolatry is inner; it is not in the streets but in the courts of the house. Corruption that reaches the inner gate is worse than corruption outside the wall. The New Testament transfers the whole architecture to the believer. Paul prays that God would grant “to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man” (Ephesians 3:16) — the strengthening is inward, invisible, and done by the Spirit, and it is what makes Christ's dwelling in the heart by faith possible. And Luke records the plainest inner room in the New Testament: the jailer “thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks” (Acts 16:24), where at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises, and the prisoners heard them.
webster_summary: Further within. The temple's inner house held the cherubim; Ezekiel finds the idol at the inner gate; Paul prays for strength in the inner man; and the inner prison at Philippi became a place of midnight singing.
webster_full: INNER, a. [comp. of in.] Interior; further inward than something else; as an inner chamber.
2. Interior; internal; not outward; as the inner man.
3. INNERMOST, a. Farthest inward; most remote from the surface or external part.
4. In Scripture, the inner court, the court of the priests; the inner house, the most holy place.
5. The inner man, the soul or spiritual nature, as distinguished from the body, Eph. 3.
corruption_summary: Inwardness is treated as the whole of religion, so that a private spirituality replaces the outward obedience Scripture requires — or else the inner man is neglected entirely for a managed exterior.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern preference for the inward runs deep, and it produces a religion that is felt but never enacted — a private spirituality with no assembly, no ordinances, no submission to elders, and no discipline. Scripture will not have it. The same Paul who prays for strength in the inner man commands baptism, the Lord's Supper, the gathering of the church, and the honouring of office. What is inward is the root; what is outward is the fruit, and a root that never produces fruit is a claim rather than a root. The opposite failure is Ezekiel's: an outward order fully maintained — a functioning temple, a busy priesthood — with an image of jealousy standing at the inner gate. Both errors are answered by the same doctrine, that God searches the heart and requires obedience of the whole man.

The principle to recover is the inner prison. It is the deepest, darkest room in the story, feet in stocks, backs laid open with rods, and it is the place from which praise came at midnight. Paul's prayer in Ephesians 3:16 is not for a comfortable interior life but for might — strength in the inner man — and Philippi shows what that strength does when the outer man has been beaten. The prisoners heard them, the earthquake came, and a jailer who had meant to kill himself was asking before dawn what he must do to be saved.

pos: a. (dense; of great depth between surfaces; rendering Hebrew arafel in thick darkness, ab in thick clouds)
etymology: From the Saxon thicce, dense. In the KJV the adjective is most often attached to darkness, clouds, boughs, and bosses — things whose density either hides or protects, which is why it becomes a word about God's nearness rather than his distance.
biblical_def: Thick in the Authorized Version is chiefly the density that hides. Its great verse is Sinai's: “And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21). The two halves are one of the sharpest contrasts in Scripture — the people stand back from the darkness, Moses walks into it, and the reason is given in four words, where God was. The thick darkness is not the absence of God but the covering of his presence; it hides him because he cannot be looked upon, and the mediator goes in. David uses the same picture in his song of deliverance: God “made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, and thick clouds of the skies” (2 Samuel 22:12) — the imagery of the storm theophany, where the density is the tent he dwells in. The word also serves the ordinary and the ominous. Job describes a man charging God like a soldier “upon the thick bosses of his bucklers” (Job 15:26), running at the Almighty behind the thickest part of a shield. And Ezekiel measures the pride of Assyria by height: a cedar in Lebanon of high stature, “and his top was among the thick boughs” (Ezekiel 31:3) — a tree so tall it stood in the canopy, and the chapter is about its felling.
webster_summary: Dense. Its chief use is the thick darkness of Sinai, which the people stood back from and Moses entered where God was — density that covers the presence rather than marking its absence.
webster_full: THICK, a. [Sax. thicce.] Dense; not thin; as a thick fluid; a thick vapor.
2. Having more depth or extent from one surface to its opposite than a certain other thing.
3. Close; crowded; set with things near to each other; as a thick forest.
4. Frequent; following each other in quick succession; as, the blows fell thick.
5. THICK, n. The thickest part, or the time when any thing is thickest; as in the thick of the fight.
corruption_summary: God's hiddenness is read as absence or as coldness, when Scripture makes the thick darkness the covering of a presence too great to be looked upon — and gives a mediator to enter it.
corruption_paragraphs: When God seems dark, the modern instinct is to conclude either that he is not there or that he is indifferent. Exodus 20:21 answers both in a single clause. The darkness was thick, the people were afraid and stood afar off — and God was in it. Divine hiddenness in Scripture is a function of glory, not of absence: he dwells in the light which no man can approach unto (1 Timothy 6:16), and the same inaccessibility can be described as blazing light or as thick cloud, because the effect on a creature's eyes is the same. This is why the classical attributes matter pastorally. A God who is simple, immutable, and infinite cannot be surveyed by us, and the dark is the shape our not-surveying takes.

The principle to recover is the mediator in the sentence. The people stood afar off; Moses drew near. Israel could not enter the darkness and was not asked to; a man went in on their behalf and came back with the words of God. Hebrews contrasts that mountain of blackness and darkness and tempest with the mount Zion believers have come to, and names the reason for the difference: Jesus the mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 12:18-24). What Moses did once and partially, Christ has done for ever, and those who are in him are brought inside the cloud rather than kept at the foot of the mountain.
roots_summary: Hebrew arafel is heavy gloom or thick darkness, the cloud of Sinai; ab is a thick cloud; abah is to be thick or dense, used of the boughs of a great tree.

Hebrew choshek (H2822) — darkness; the general term, distinguished from the thick arafel.
Greek gnophos (G1105) — blackness, thick gloom; the word for Sinai's darkness in Hebrews 12:18.
